input:
No longer mourn for me when I am dead,  
Than you shall hear the bitter bell  
Warn the world that I have fled  
From this vile world with wretched worms to dwell:  
Nay if you read this line, remember not,  
The hand that writ it, for I love you so,  
That I in your sweet thoughts would be forgot,  
If thinking on me then should make you woe.
target:
Yet this thy praise cannot be so thy praise,
To tie up envy, evermore enlarged,
  If some suspect of ill masked not thy show,
  Then thou alone kingdoms of hearts shouldst owe.


                    71

No longer mourn for me when I am dead,
Than you shall hear the surly sullen bell
Give warning to the world that I am fled
From this vile world with vilest worms to dwell:
Nay if you read this line, remember not,
The hand that writ it, for I love you so,
That I in your sweet thoughts would be forgot,
If thinking on me then should make you woe.

input:
O if you look upon this verse,  
When I, perhaps, have been mixed with clay,  
Do not even recite my name;  
Let your love fade even with my life.  
Lest the world take notice of your sorrow,  
And mock you after I am gone.  

O let the world task you to recite,  
What merit lived in me that you should love  
After my death, dear love, forget me quite,  
For you in me can prove nothing worthy.  
Unless you would craft a lie of virtue,  
To do more for me than mine own desert.
target:
O if, I say, you look upon this verse,
When I (perhaps) compounded am with clay,
Do not so much as my poor name rehearse;
But let your love even with my life decay.
  Lest the wise world should look into your moan,
  And mock you with me after I am gone.


                    72

O lest the world should task you to recite,
What merit lived in me that you should love
After my death, dear love, forget me quite,
For you in me can nothing worthy prove.
Unless you would devise some virtuous lie,
To do more for me than mine own desert,

input:
And let the praise of the departed be weighed more heavily than the truth that would willingly share,  
For if your true love seems unfaithful in this,  
you shall speak well of me in love, though it be untrue,  
my name shall be buried where my body lies,  
and live no more to shame nor me, nor you.  
For I am shamed by what I bring forth,  
and so should you, to love things nothing worth.  

That time of year thou mayst in me behold,  
when yellow leaves, or none, or few do hang  
upon those boughs that shake against the chill,  
bare ruined choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.
target:
And hang more praise upon deceased I,
Than niggard truth would willingly impart:
O lest your true love may seem false in this,
That you for love speak well of me untrue,
My name be buried where my body is,
And live no more to shame nor me, nor you.
  For I am shamed by that which I bring forth,
  And so should you, to love things nothing worth.


                    73

That time of year thou mayst in me behold,
When yellow leaves, or none, or few do hang
Upon those boughs which shake against the cold,
Bare ruined choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.

input:
In me you see the fading of such a day,  
As the sun sets and fades in the west,  
Which gradually takes away the dark night,  
Death's second self that seals everything in eternal rest.  
In me you see the glowing of such a fire,  
That lies on the ashes of his youth,  
As the death-bed where it must expire,  
Consumed by the very thing it was nourished by.  
This you perceive, which makes your love more strong,  
To love that well, which you must leave soon.  

But be contented when that fall in arrest,  
Without any bail shall take me away.
target:
In me thou seest the twilight of such day,
As after sunset fadeth in the west,
Which by and by black night doth take away,
Death’s second self that seals up all in rest.
In me thou seest the glowing of such fire,
That on the ashes of his youth doth lie,
As the death-bed, whereon it must expire,
Consumed with that which it was nourished by.
  This thou perceiv’st, which makes thy love more strong,
  To love that well, which thou must leave ere long.


                    74

But be contented when that fell arrest,
Without all bail shall carry me away,

input: When you review this, you are reviewing the very part that was consecrated to you, the earth can have only earth, which is its due, my spirit is your better part than me, so then you have only lost the final remnants of life, the prey of worms, my body having been consumed, the cowardly conquest of a wretch's knife, too base for you to be remembered, the worth of that is what it contains, and that is this, and this remains with you.
target:
My life hath in this line some interest,
Which for memorial still with thee shall stay.
When thou reviewest this, thou dost review,
The very part was consecrate to thee,
The earth can have but earth, which is his due,
My spirit is thine the better part of me,
So then thou hast but lost the dregs of life,
The prey of worms, my body being dead,
The coward conquest of a wretch’s knife,
Too base of thee to be remembered,
  The worth of that, is that which it contains,
  And that is this, and this with thee remains.


                    75

input:
And for your peace, I wrestle with such a struggle,  
As ’twixt a miser and his wealth is found.  
Now proud as an enjoyer, and anon,  
Doubting the filching age will steal his treasure,  
Now counting best to be with you alone,  
Then bettered that the world may see my pleasure,  
Sometime all full with feasting on your sight,  
And by and by clean starved for a look,  
Possessing or pursuing no delight  
Save what is had, or must from you be took.
target:
So are you to my thoughts as food to life,
Or as sweet-seasoned showers are to the ground;
And for the peace of you I hold such strife
As ’twixt a miser and his wealth is found.
Now proud as an enjoyer, and anon
Doubting the filching age will steal his treasure,
Now counting best to be with you alone,
Then bettered that the world may see my pleasure,
Sometime all full with feasting on your sight,
And by and by clean starved for a look,
Possessing or pursuing no delight
Save what is had, or must from you be took.

input:
Thus do I pine and overindulge day by day,  
Or feast upon all, or all be consumed.  

Why is my verse so barren of new pride?  
So far from variation or quick change?  
Why with the time do I not glance aside  
To new-found methods, and to compounds strange?  
Why write I still all one, ever the same,  
And keep invention in a noted weed,  
That every word doth almost tell my name,  
Showing their birth, and where they did proceed?  
O know sweet love I always write of you,  
And you and love are still my argument:  
So all my best is dressing old words new.
target:
Thus do I pine and surfeit day by day,
  Or gluttoning on all, or all away.


                    76

Why is my verse so barren of new pride?
So far from variation or quick change?
Why with the time do I not glance aside
To new-found methods, and to compounds strange?
Why write I still all one, ever the same,
And keep invention in a noted weed,
That every word doth almost tell my name,
Showing their birth, and where they did proceed?
O know sweet love I always write of you,
And you and love are still my argument:
So all my best is dressing old words new,

input:
I'm spending what's already been spent  
For as the sun is daily new and old,  
So is my love still telling what is told.  

Your mirror will show you how your beauties fade,  
Your dial how your precious minutes waste,  
These vacant leaves your mind's imprint will bear,  
And of this book, this learning mayst you taste.  
The wrinkles in your mirror will truly show,  
Of mouthed graves will give you memory,  
You by your dial's hidden actions mayst know,  
Time's cunning progress to eternity.  
Look what your memory cannot contain,  
Leave these empty spaces, and you will find.
target:
Spending again what is already spent:
  For as the sun is daily new and old,
  So is my love still telling what is told.


                    77

Thy glass will show thee how thy beauties wear,
Thy dial how thy precious minutes waste,
These vacant leaves thy mind’s imprint will bear,
And of this book, this learning mayst thou taste.
The wrinkles which thy glass will truly show,
Of mouthed graves will give thee memory,
Thou by thy dial’s shady stealth mayst know,
Time’s thievish progress to eternity.
Look what thy memory cannot contain,
Commit to these waste blanks, and thou shalt find

input:
Those children, nurtured and delivered from thy mind,  
Have taken a new acquaintance of thy thoughts.  
These duties, so often as thou wilt gaze,  
Shall benefit thee, and greatly enrich thy work.  

So often have I invoked thee as my muse,  
And found such fair aid in my verse,  
As every alien pen hath sought my use,  
And under thee their poetry has been dispersed.  
Thy eyes, that taught the mute to sing above,  
And heavy ignorance to fly aloft,  
Have added feathers to the learned’s wing,  
And given grace a double majesty.  
Yet be most proud of that which I compile.
target:
Those children nursed, delivered from thy brain,
To take a new acquaintance of thy mind.
  These offices, so oft as thou wilt look,
  Shall profit thee, and much enrich thy book.


                    78

So oft have I invoked thee for my muse,
And found such fair assistance in my verse,
As every alien pen hath got my use,
And under thee their poesy disperse.
Thine eyes, that taught the dumb on high to sing,
And heavy ignorance aloft to fly,
Have added feathers to the learned’s wing,
And given grace a double majesty.
Yet be most proud of that which I compile,

input:
Whose influence is yours, and born from you,  
You mend the style of others but not their art,  
And your talents adorn the skills of all.  
Yet you are all my art, and rise to the height of learning, my unrefined ignorance.  

While I alone called upon your aid,  
My verse once held your gentle grace,  
But now my numbers decay, and my ailing muse gives way to another place.  
I grant (sweet love) your argument deserves the effort of a better pen,  
Yet what of you, your poet invents,  
He takes it from you and gives it back to you.
target:
Whose influence is thine, and born of thee,
In others’ works thou dost but mend the style,
And arts with thy sweet graces graced be.
  But thou art all my art, and dost advance
  As high as learning, my rude ignorance.


                    79

Whilst I alone did call upon thy aid,
My verse alone had all thy gentle grace,
But now my gracious numbers are decayed,
And my sick muse doth give an other place.
I grant (sweet love) thy lovely argument
Deserves the travail of a worthier pen,
Yet what of thee thy poet doth invent,
He robs thee of, and pays it thee again,

input:
He bestows virtue and appropriates the word,  
bestowing beauty upon you,  
discovering it in your cheek: he can offer no praise,  
but what resides within you.  
Do not thank him for what he says,  
for what he owes you, you yourself pay.  

I feel overwhelmed when writing of you,  
knowing a more virtuous spirit uses your name,  
spending all his energy to make me hesitant to speak of your fame.  
Yet your worth is as vast as the ocean,  
the humblest as the proudest sail bear it.
target:
He lends thee virtue, and he stole that word,
From thy behaviour, beauty doth he give
And found it in thy cheek: he can afford
No praise to thee, but what in thee doth live.
  Then thank him not for that which he doth say,
  Since what he owes thee, thou thyself dost pay.


                    80

O how I faint when I of you do write,
Knowing a better spirit doth use your name,
And in the praise thereof spends all his might,
To make me tongue-tied speaking of your fame.
But since your worth, wide as the ocean is,
The humble as the proudest sail doth bear,

input:
My sassy hull (inferior far to his)  
Does boldly appear on your broad main deck.  
Your least support will hold me afloat,  
While he rides upon your soundless deep,  
Or (being wrecked) I am a worthless boat,  
He of towering structure, and of goodly pride.  
Then if he thrives and I be cast away,  
The worst was this—my love was my decay.  

Or I shall live your epitaph to make,  
Or you survive when I in earth am rotten,  
From hence your memory death cannot take,  
Although in me each part will be forgotten.  
Your name from hence immortal life shall have.
target:
My saucy bark (inferior far to his)
On your broad main doth wilfully appear.
Your shallowest help will hold me up afloat,
Whilst he upon your soundless deep doth ride,
Or (being wrecked) I am a worthless boat,
He of tall building, and of goodly pride.
  Then if he thrive and I be cast away,
  The worst was this: my love was my decay.


                    81

Or I shall live your epitaph to make,
Or you survive when I in earth am rotten,
From hence your memory death cannot take,
Although in me each part will be forgotten.
Your name from hence immortal life shall have,

input:
Though I (once gone) to all the world must die,  
The earth can yield me but an ordinary grave,  
When you are buried in the eyes of men,  
Your monument shall be my gentle verse,  
Which eyes not yet created shall read aloud,  
And tongues to be, your being shall rehearse,  
When all the breathers of this world are dead,  
You will still live, such virtue hath my pen,  
Where breath most breathes, even in the mouths of men.  

I grant thou wert not married to my muse,  
And therefore mayst without being tainted  
The dedicated words which writers use  
Of their fair subject, blessing every book.
target:
Though I (once gone) to all the world must die,
The earth can yield me but a common grave,
When you entombed in men’s eyes shall lie,
Your monument shall be my gentle verse,
Which eyes not yet created shall o’er-read,
And tongues to be, your being shall rehearse,
When all the breathers of this world are dead,
  You still shall live, such virtue hath my pen,
  Where breath most breathes, even in the mouths of men.


                    82

I grant thou wert not married to my muse,
And therefore mayst without attaint o’erlook
The dedicated words which writers use
Of their fair subject, blessing every book.

input:
I never saw that you needed painting,  
and therefore to your fair no painting set,  
I found (or thought I found) you did exceed.
target:
Thou art as fair in knowledge as in hue,
Finding thy worth a limit past my praise,
And therefore art enforced to seek anew,
Some fresher stamp of the time-bettering days.
And do so love, yet when they have devised,
What strained touches rhetoric can lend,
Thou truly fair, wert truly sympathized,
In true plain words, by thy true-telling friend.
  And their gross painting might be better used,
  Where cheeks need blood, in thee it is abused.


                    83

I never saw that you did painting need,
And therefore to your fair no painting set,
I found (or thought I found) you did exceed,

input:
That empty tender of a poet’s debt:  
And therefore have I rested on your report,  
That you yourself, being alive, might show,  
How far a modern quill does fall short,  
Speaking of worth, what worth in you grows.  
This silence for my sin you assigned blame,  
Which shall be most my glory being mute,  
For I do not harm beauty being still,  
When others would give life, and bring a tomb.  
There lives more life in one of your fair eyes,  
Than both your poets can create in praise.  
Who is it that says most, which can say more?
target:
That barren tender of a poet’s debt:
And therefore have I slept in your report,
That you yourself being extant well might show,
How far a modern quill doth come too short,
Speaking of worth, what worth in you doth grow.
This silence for my sin you did impute,
Which shall be most my glory being dumb,
For I impair not beauty being mute,
When others would give life, and bring a tomb.
  There lives more life in one of your fair eyes,
  Than both your poets can in praise devise.


                    84

Who is it that says most, which can say more,

input:
Let him copy what you’ve written,  
Not making worse what nature made so clear,  
And such a counterpart shall fame his wit,  
Making his style admired everywhere.  
You to your beauteous blessings add a curse,  
Being fond on praise, which makes your praises worse.
target:
Than this rich praise: that you alone are you,
In whose confine immured is the store,
Which should example where your equal grew.
Lean penury within that pen doth dwell,
That to his subject lends not some small glory,
But he that writes of you, if he can tell,
That you are you, so dignifies his story.
Let him but copy what in you is writ,
Not making worse what nature made so clear,
And such a counterpart shall fame his wit,
Making his style admired every where.
  You to your beauteous blessings add a curse,
  Being fond on praise, which makes your praises worse.

input:
My hesitant muse, in manners, remains still,  
While your praise, richly compiled, preserves its essence with a golden pen,  
And precious phrases, collected by all the Muses, are etched in polished form.  
I think good thoughts, while others write good words,  
And like a simple scribe, recite 'Amen' to every hymn that a capable spirit offers.  
Hearing your praise, I say, 'It is so, it is true,'  
And to the most of praise, add something more,  
But that is in my thought, whose love to you  
(Though words come last) holds its rank before,  
Then others, for the breath of words, respect.
target:
85

My tongue-tied muse in manners holds her still,
While comments of your praise richly compiled,
Reserve their character with golden quill,
And precious phrase by all the Muses filed.
I think good thoughts, whilst other write good words,
And like unlettered clerk still cry Amen,
To every hymn that able spirit affords,
In polished form of well refined pen.
Hearing you praised, I say ’tis so, ’tis true,
And to the most of praise add something more,
But that is in my thought, whose love to you
(Though words come hindmost) holds his rank before,
  Then others, for the breath of words respect,

input:
Was it the prideful sail of his great verse,  
Bound for the prize of (all too precious) you,  
That buried my ripe thoughts in my brain,  
Making their tomb the womb wherein they grew?  
Was it his spirit, taught by spirits to write,  
Above the limits of mortal skill,  
That struck me dead?  
No, neither he, nor his compeers by night,  
Who offered aid to my verse, astonished.  
He nor that affable familiar ghost,  
Which nightly gulls him with intelligence,  
As victors of my silence cannot boast,  
I was not sick of any fear from thence.
target:
Me for my dumb thoughts, speaking in effect.


                    86

Was it the proud full sail of his great verse,
Bound for the prize of (all too precious) you,
That did my ripe thoughts in my brain inhearse,
Making their tomb the womb wherein they grew?
Was it his spirit, by spirits taught to write,
Above a mortal pitch, that struck me dead?
No, neither he, nor his compeers by night
Giving him aid, my verse astonished.
He nor that affable familiar ghost
Which nightly gulls him with intelligence,
As victors of my silence cannot boast,
I was not sick of any fear from thence.

input:
Farewell! You are too valuable to be owned by me,  
And like enough, you know your worth,  
The proof of your worth gives you freedom,  
My ties to you are all fixed.  
How can I keep you but through your consent,  
And for that value, where is my due?  
The reason for this valuable gift in me is lacking,  
And so my license to keep you is turning back, not in the right direction.  
You gave yourself, and then didn't know your own worth,  
Or to me, you gave it, else you were mistaken.
target:
But when your countenance filled up his line,
  Then lacked I matter, that enfeebled mine.


                    87

Farewell! thou art too dear for my possessing,
And like enough thou know’st thy estimate,
The charter of thy worth gives thee releasing:
My bonds in thee are all determinate.
For how do I hold thee but by thy granting,
And for that riches where is my deserving?
The cause of this fair gift in me is wanting,
And so my patent back again is swerving.
Thyself thou gav’st, thy own worth then not knowing,
Or me to whom thou gav’st it, else mistaking,

input:
When you're disposed to overlook me,  
And place my merit in the eye of contempt,  
I'll confront you, against myself,  
And prove you virtuous, though you're forsworn:  
With my own weaknesses best acquainted,  
I'll set down a story of concealed faults,  
Convicted of them, where I am attainted:  
That you, in losing me, shall win much glory.
target:
So thy great gift upon misprision growing,
Comes home again, on better judgement making.
  Thus have I had thee as a dream doth flatter,
  In sleep a king, but waking no such matter.


                    88

When thou shalt be disposed to set me light,
And place my merit in the eye of scorn,
Upon thy side, against my self I’ll fight,
And prove thee virtuous, though thou art forsworn:
With mine own weakness being best acquainted,
Upon thy part I can set down a story
Of faults concealed, wherein I am attainted:
That thou in losing me, shalt win much glory:

input:
And I will gain from this,  
For focusing all my loving thoughts on you,  
The injuries I inflict on myself are a benefit to you, doubling my advantage.  
My love is so profound that I belong to you,  
That for your sake, I will endure all harm.  

If you claim you abandoned me for a reason,  
I will address that offense,  
Speak of my inability to walk, and I will stop immediately:  
Without defending my own reasons.  
You cannot disgrace me as much as I will disgrace myself, knowing your will.
target:
And I by this will be a gainer too,
For bending all my loving thoughts on thee,
The injuries that to my self I do,
Doing thee vantage, double-vantage me.
  Such is my love, to thee I so belong,
  That for thy right, my self will bear all wrong.


                    89

Say that thou didst forsake me for some fault,
And I will comment upon that offence,
Speak of my lameness, and I straight will halt:
Against thy reasons making no defence.
Thou canst not (love) disgrace me half so ill,
To set a form upon desired change,
As I’ll my self disgrace, knowing thy will,

input:
Then hate me when you will, if ever, now,  
now while the world is in turmoil, my deeds will cross,  
join with the spite of fortune, make me bow,  
and do not let me be dropped in for an after-loss:  
ah, do not let me be dropped in for an after-loss,  
when my heart has escaped this sorrow.
target:
I will acquaintance strangle and look strange:
Be absent from thy walks and in my tongue,
Thy sweet beloved name no more shall dwell,
Lest I, too much profane, should do it wrong,
And haply of our old acquaintance tell.
  For thee, against my self I’ll vow debate,
  For I must ne’er love him whom thou dost hate.


                    90

Then hate me when thou wilt, if ever, now,
Now while the world is bent my deeds to cross,
join with the spite of fortune, make me bow,
And do not drop in for an after-loss:
Ah do not, when my heart hath ’scaped this sorrow,

input:
Come from the rear of a conquered sorrow,  
Do not let a windy night spoil a rainy morning,  
To linger out a planned defeat.  
If you will leave me, do not leave me last,  
When other minor sorrows have finished their resentment,  
But in the beginning come, so shall I taste  
At first the very worst of fortune’s might.  
And other sources of sorrow, which now seem sorrow,  
Will not feel as bad as the loss of thee.  

Some take pride in their lineage, some in their talents,  
Some in their riches, some in their physical prowess,  
Some in their attire, even if it’s somewhat outdated.
target:
Come in the rearward of a conquered woe,
Give not a windy night a rainy morrow,
To linger out a purposed overthrow.
If thou wilt leave me, do not leave me last,
When other petty griefs have done their spite,
But in the onset come, so shall I taste
At first the very worst of fortune’s might.
  And other strains of woe, which now seem woe,
  Compared with loss of thee, will not seem so.


                    91

Some glory in their birth, some in their skill,
Some in their wealth, some in their body’s force,
Some in their garments though new-fangled ill:

input:
But do your worst to steal yourself away,  
For the term of life, you are mine.
target:
Some in their hawks and hounds, some in their horse.
And every humour hath his adjunct pleasure,
Wherein it finds a joy above the rest,
But these particulars are not my measure,
All these I better in one general best.
Thy love is better than high birth to me,
Richer than wealth, prouder than garments’ costs,
Of more delight than hawks and horses be:
And having thee, of all men’s pride I boast.
  Wretched in this alone, that thou mayst take,
  All this away, and me most wretched make.


                    92

But do thy worst to steal thyself away,
For term of life thou art assured mine,

input:
And life will not last longer than your love,  
For it depends on your love.  
Then I need not fear the worst of harm,  
When my life ends in the least of them,  
I notice a better situation belongs  
Than what depends on your mood.  
You cannot vex me with a shifting heart,  
Since my life lies in your rebellion,  
O what a happy name do I find,  
Happy to have your love, happy to die!  
But what is so blessed and fair that is free from blame?  
You may be false, and yet I don't know.
target:
And life no longer than thy love will stay,
For it depends upon that love of thine.
Then need I not to fear the worst of wrongs,
When in the least of them my life hath end,
I see, a better state to me belongs
Than that, which on thy humour doth depend.
Thou canst not vex me with inconstant mind,
Since that my life on thy revolt doth lie,
O what a happy title do I find,
Happy to have thy love, happy to die!
  But what’s so blessed-fair that fears no blot?
  Thou mayst be false, and yet I know it not.

input:
So I shall live, assuming you are true,  
like a deceived husband, where love’s face still appears,  
even though changed, to me it may still seem love.  
Your looks, your heart in another place.  
For there can be no hatred in your eye,  
so I cannot know your change,  
for in many eyes, the false heart’s history  
is written in varied expressions and wrinkles.  
But the heavens have ordained that in your face,  
sweet love shall ever dwell,  
no matter what your thoughts or heart’s workings are,  
your looks shall tell nothing but sweetness.  
How like Eve’s apple doth thy beauty grow.
target:
93

So shall I live, supposing thou art true,
Like a deceived husband, so love’s face,
May still seem love to me, though altered new:
Thy looks with me, thy heart in other place.
For there can live no hatred in thine eye,
Therefore in that I cannot know thy change,
In many’s looks, the false heart’s history
Is writ in moods and frowns and wrinkles strange.
But heaven in thy creation did decree,
That in thy face sweet love should ever dwell,
Whate’er thy thoughts, or thy heart’s workings be,
Thy looks should nothing thence, but sweetness tell.
  How like Eve’s apple doth thy beauty grow,

input:
If your noble virtue does not match your display,  
Those who hold the power to harm yet choose to stay  
Who, by their own motion, leave others to be moved,  
Unmoved by temptation, cold and slow to yield:  
They rightly inherit heaven’s most precious gifts,  
And wield nature’s wealth without waste or greed,  
They are the lords and stewards of their own face,  
Others, but caretakers of their highest grace:  
The most beautiful flower, yet prone to decay,  
And the most vile weed that dares to surpass its grace.
target:
If thy sweet virtue answer not thy show.


                    94

They that have power to hurt, and will do none,
That do not do the thing, they most do show,
Who moving others, are themselves as stone,
Unmoved, cold, and to temptation slow:
They rightly do inherit heaven’s graces,
And husband nature’s riches from expense,

O the benefit of ill, now I see that better is, by evil still made better.  
The love once ruined, when rebuilt anew, grows fairer, stronger, far greater.

target:
Nor taste, nor smell, desire to be invited
To any sensual feast with thee alone:
But my five wits, nor my five senses can
Dissuade one foolish heart from serving thee,
Who leaves unswayed the likeness of a man,
Thy proud heart’s slave and vassal wretch to be:
  Only my plague thus far I count my gain,
  That she that makes me sin, awards me pain.

I love you lawfully, as you love those whom your eyes woo as I plead for you,  
plant pity in your heart that when it grows,  
your pity may deserve to be pitied.  
If you try to claim what you hide,  
you might be denied by your own example.
target:
Or if it do, not from those lips of thine,
That have profaned their scarlet ornaments,
And sealed false bonds of love as oft as mine,
Robbed others’ beds’ revenues of their rents.
Be it lawful I love thee as thou lov’st those,
Whom thine eyes woo as mine importune thee,
Root pity in thy heart that when it grows,
Thy pity may deserve to pitied be.
  If thou dost seek to have what thou dost hide,

Sets down her babe and makes all swift dispatch

input:
Two loves I have, of comfort and despair,  
Whilst her neglected child holds her in chase,  
Cries to catch her whose busy care is bent,  
To follow that which flies before her face:  
Not prizing her poor infant’s discontent;  
So run’st thou after that which flies from thee,  
Whilst I thy babe chase thee afar behind,  
But if thou catch thy hope turn back to me:  
And play the mother’s part, kiss me, be kind.  
So will I pray that thou mayst have thy Will,  
If thou turn back and my loud crying still.

Two loves I have, of comfort and despair,

input:
The better angel is a man who is fair,  
the worse spirit a woman with a dull complexion.  
To win me soon to hell my female evil  
tempteth my better angel from my side,  
and would corrupt my saint to be a devil,  
wooing his purity with her foul pride.  
And whether that my angel be turned fiend,  
I may suspect, yet not directly tell;  
but being both from me both to each friend,  
I guess one angel in another’s hell.  
Yet this shall I ne’er know, but live in doubt,  
till my bad angel burns out my good one.

input:
A poor soul, the heart of my sinful world,  
Whose lips, crafted by love's own hand,  
Spoke the words 'I hate' to me,  
Who mourned for her sake,  
Yet when she saw my plight,  
Mercy took root in her heart,  
Rebuking the tongue that once was sweet,  
Used to deliver harsh judgments,  
And taught it anew, to greet with gentleness,  
'I hate' she altered with an ending,  
As gentle day follows night,  
Which like a fiend flies from heaven to hell.  
She threw 'I hate' away, saving my life by saying 'not you.'

Those lips that Love’s own hand did make,
Breathed forth the sound that said ‘I hate’,
To me that languished for her sake:
But when she saw my woeful state,
Straight in her heart did mercy come,
Chiding that tongue that ever sweet,
Was used in giving gentle doom:
And taught it thus anew to greet:
‘I hate’ she altered with an end,
That followed it as gentle day,
Doth follow night who like a fiend
From heaven to hell is flown away.
  ‘I hate’, from hate away she threw,
  And saved my life saying ‘not you’.


                    146

Poor soul the centre of my sinful earth,

input:
My sinful earth now hosts rebellious forces,  
Why do you suffer from inner pain and lack,  
Painting your outward walls with expensive and flashy hues?  
Why spend such a costly price on a fading estate,  
When your lifespan is so brief?  
Will worms inheritors of this excess  
Eat up your expenses? Is this your body’s end?  
Then your soul lives on through your servant’s loss,  
And let that pine to increase your wealth;  
Buy divine terms in the sale of worthless hours;  
Be nourished within, be rich no more without.  
So shall you feed on death, that feeds on humans,  
And death once dead, there's no more dying left.
target:
My sinful earth these rebel powers array,
Why dost thou pine within and suffer dearth
Painting thy outward walls so costly gay?
Why so large cost having so short a lease,
Dost thou upon thy fading mansion spend?
Shall worms inheritors of this excess
Eat up thy charge? is this thy body’s end?
Then soul live thou upon thy servant’s loss,
And let that pine to aggravate thy store;
Buy terms divine in selling hours of dross;
Within be fed, without be rich no more,
  So shall thou feed on death, that feeds on men,

My love is a fever that never stills,  
rooted in the sickness it prolongs,  
feeding on the things that keep the ill,  
serving the uncertain appetite to please:  
my rational mind, the doctor of my love,  
frustrated because his advice is not kept,  
has left me, and I now approve my despair,  
desire is death, which physic once could cure.  
I’ve reached the point where my rational mind has given up,  
and madness now consumes me,  
my thoughts and words as chaotic as those of madmen,  
spilling truth vainly expressed.  
For I’ve vowed to you, a beacon of light,  
yet you are as dark as hell, as black as night.
target:
147

My love is as a fever longing still,
For that which longer nurseth the disease,
Feeding on that which doth preserve the ill,
Th’ uncertain sickly appetite to please:
My reason the physician to my love,
Angry that his prescriptions are not kept
Hath left me, and I desperate now approve,
Desire is death, which physic did except.
Past cure I am, now reason is past care,
And frantic-mad with evermore unrest,
My thoughts and my discourse as mad men’s are,
At random from the truth vainly expressed.
  For I have sworn thee fair, and thought thee bright,
  Who art as black as hell, as dark as night.

What eyes has love placed in my mind,  
Which lack the alignment of true sight,  
If they do, where has my judgment gone,  
That condemns falsely what they see correctly?  
If that is fair where my false eyes fancy,  
What does the world imply when it says it is not so?  
If it is not, then love shows that love's eye is not so true as all men's: no, how can it?  
How can love's eye be true, so troubled by watching and tears?  
It's not surprising that I mistake my view,  
The sun itself does not see until heaven clears.

O me! what eyes hath love put in my head,
Which have no correspondence with true sight,
Or if they have, where is my judgement fled,
That censures falsely what they see aright?
If that be fair whereon my false eyes dote,
What means the world to say it is not so?
If it be not, then love doth well denote,
Love’s eye is not so true as all men’s: no,
How can it? O how can love’s eye be true,
That is so vexed with watching and with tears?
No marvel then though I mistake my view,
The sun it self sees not, till heaven clears.

input:
Can you, O cruel, say I do not love you when I share my own pain with you?  
Do I not think of you when I forget that I am, in my own self, an all-tyrant for your sake?  
Who hates you that I call my friend, on whom you frown, but I bow to you?  
If you look down on me, I do not spend revenge on myself with a present moan?  
What worth do I hold in myself that is so proud to despise your service?
target:
O cunning love, with tears thou keep’st me blind,
  Lest eyes well-seeing thy foul faults should find.

On whom frown’st thou that I do fawn upon,

input:
From where does this powerful power come?  
Guided by the movement of your gaze?  
Yet love and hate—now I know your mind,  
Those who see your love, and I remain blind.  
From where does this troubling quality come?  
In the very refuse of your deeds,  
There lies such strength and warrant of skill,  
That in my mind, your worst is better than your best.
target:
When all my best doth worship thy defect,
Commanded by the motion of thine eyes?
  But love hate on for now I know thy mind,
  Those that can see thou lov’st, and I am blind.

O from what power hast thou this powerful might,
With insufficiency my heart to sway,
To make me give the lie to my true sight,
And swear that brightness doth not grace the day?
Whence hast thou this becoming of things ill,
That in the very refuse of thy deeds,
There is such strength and warrantise of skill,
That in my mind thy worst all best exceeds?

Who taught you how to make me love you more,  
The more I hear and see just cause of hate?  
O though I love what others do abhor,  
With others thou shouldst not abhor my state.  
If thy unworthiness raised love in me,  
More worthy I to be beloved of thee.  

Love is too young to know what conscience is,

Then gentle cheater urge not my amiss,  
Lest guilty of my faults thy sweet self prove.  
For thou betraying me, I do betray  
My nobler part to my gross body’s treason.

My soul tells my body that he may,  
Love triumphs in flesh, yet reason fades,  
At his name's call, he points out the prize,  
A victory proud of his own pride,  
Content to be my servant,  
To stand in your affairs, fall by your side.

But why do I condemn thee for breaking two oaths,  
when I myself have broken twenty? I am most perjured,  
for all my vows are but to mislead thee:  
and all my honest faith in thee is lost.

A fire that ignites the heart was placed beside him,  
while many nymphs, who had vowed to live chaste lives,  
came trailing by, but in her hand that was pure,  
the most beautiful devotee took up that flame,  
which had warmed many hearts of true and steadfast love,  
and so the general of desire,  
was sleeping by a hand that had been freed from its restraint.  
This flame was quenched in a cool well,  
from the fire of love, it absorbed heat forever,  
growing into a bath and a remedy for the sick.  
But I, my mistress’ servant,  
came there for cure and this, by that I prove,  
that love’s fire heats water, but water cannot cool love.
target:
Laid by his side his heart-inflaming brand,
Whilst many nymphs that vowed chaste life to keep,
Came tripping by, but in her maiden hand,
The fairest votary took up that fire,
Which many legions of true hearts had warmed,
And so the general of hot desire,
Was sleeping by a virgin hand disarmed.
This brand she quenched in a cool well by,
Which from Love’s fire took heat perpetual,
Growing a bath and healthful remedy,
For men diseased; but I, my mistress’ thrall,
  Came there for cure and this by that I prove,
  Love’s fire heats water, water cools not love.

input: Pompey: I do not know, Menas, how minor grievances may be overcome by greater ones. Had it not been that we stand against them all, they would have reconciled themselves to one another. For they have already had sufficient cause to draw their swords. Yet how the fear of us may bind up their petty differences, and cement their divisions, we yet do not know. Let it be as our gods would have it! Our lives depend solely upon our strongest hands. Come, Menas.
target:

’Twere pregnant they should square between themselves,
For they have entertained cause enough
To draw their swords. But how the fear of us
May cement their divisions, and bind up
The petty difference, we yet not know.

Our lives upon to use our strongest hands.

input: The scene begins near Oliver's house, later extending into the usurper's court and the Forest of Arden. The lords belonging to the two dukes, along with pages, foresters, and other attendants, gather in this space. The god of love, represented by a person, stands among them. The dukes—Ferdinand, exiled, and Frederick, his brother and usurper—stand in contrast, their domains divided. Charles, Frederick's wrestler, and Le Beau, a courtier, serve as symbols of the struggle. The shepherds, Corin, Silvius, and Phoebe, and the country wench Audrey, along with William, a country fellow in love with her, embody the pastoral and human elements. Sir Oliver Martext, a vicar, watches over the scene, reflecting the moral and spiritual tensions.

Scene V. Another part of the Forest  

Enter Amiens, Jaques, and others.  

AMIENS.

Under the greenwood tree,  
Who loves to lie with me  
And turn his merry note  
Unto the sweet bird’s throat,  
Come hither, come hither, come hither!

No enemy  
But winter and rough weather.

More, more, I prithee, more.

It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.
